LOUISIANA
The Story of the Levees
The walls that hold back a river.
PROLOGUE
Before the levees

The Mississippi flooded wherever it pleased. It carried sediment. It built wetlands. It built Louisiana.

The river was creator and destroyer, long before anyone tried to choose which.

The river that built a state

Louisiana is not older than the river. Louisiana is what the river made.

Every acre of dry ground here was floodwater once.

CHAPTER ONE
Learning to live with water

Indigenous communities read the river's patterns first. Settlers followed, building the earliest embankments by hand. As towns became cities, the earthworks grew with them.

The first levees were not engineering. They were listening.

Building, mile by mile

Commerce needed a river that stayed where it was told. Statewide coordination turned isolated embankments into a system.

No single levee protects a state. Only a system does.

CHAPTER TWO
1927

The river broke through in more than 145 places. Hundreds of thousands lost their homes. The nation could no longer treat flood control as a local problem.

The flood that rewrote the rules.

After the water receded

Congress passed the Flood Control Act of 1928. For the first time, the federal government took responsibility for the Mississippi.

1927 didn't just flood Louisiana. It flooded the old way of thinking about the river.

CHAPTER THREE
Engineering the impossible

Levees. Floodwalls. Spillways. Pump stations. And one decision that mattered more than the rest: keeping the Mississippi from abandoning its own channel for the shorter, steeper Atchafalaya.

New Orleans exists today because a gate was built to hold a river's decision.

The Old River decision

The structure is monitored day and night. If it ever failed, the river would leave Baton Rouge and New Orleans behind within years.

Some decisions are made once and defended forever.

CHAPTER FOUR
Living behind the levee

Schools open. Farmers plant. Ports load and unload. Then Katrina arrived, and a hurricane, not the river, breached the system. The lesson landed the same way: flood protection is never finished.

Nobody thinks about the levee on a good day. That's the point.

Built to be opened

When the river runs high, the spillway takes the pressure off the city. Water is given somewhere to go, on purpose.

Sometimes protecting a city means giving the river an exit.

CHAPTER FIVE
The cost of control

Levees stopped the river from replenishing its wetlands. Without new sediment, Louisiana loses coastline faster than almost anywhere on Earth.

Every wall that protects one place stops feeding another.

Restoring the future

Sediment diversions are reconnecting the river to its wetlands. New land is being built on purpose, for the first time in a century.

The same river that built Louisiana is being asked to build it again.

The river never stops

Always moving. Always changing. Always testing the system built to contain it. The river built Louisiana. The people keep learning how to stay.

How do you live beside a river powerful enough to build your home, and powerful enough to take it away?

“The Mississippi built Louisiana. The levees made it possible for Louisiana to stay.”

THE STORY OF THE LEVEES
